extracted.intended_audience: literate general readers of The Spectator (early-18th-century readership)
extracted.subtask_description: A set of periodical-essay prescriptions and observations about polite behaviour: how to manage courtship, preserve good-humour in country company, and avoid/understand scandal and defamation. Practical moral guidance and social tactics aimed at readers navigating society and households.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect coordinated/covert courtship tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Be on guard against two persons who cooperate so that one affects ardour and the other indifference (the Damon–Strephon plot), thereby manipulating a woman's affections by contrast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signs: the seemingly indifferent man appears after the ardent one has 'tired' her; they compare notes about her carriage; contrived notes or billets to observe her response. Advice: examine your heart before yielding, watch for patterns (one who shuns you appearing everywhere, visits timed after another’s demonstrative play), and take precautions against a rival who courts by appearing amiable before he declares passion. Example/anti-pattern: turning away scornfully at a billet signed by the ostensible lover may encourage the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Win a sensible woman by agreeable general conduct, not overt rapture
rubrics_metrics.description: A sensible woman values desire over pity and is not moved merely by expressions of rapture or adoration; therefore the effective approach is that a man's general behaviour should be pleasing without addressing the woman in extravagant terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be the object of desire rather than the object of pity: cultivate agreeable manners and a composed, genteel presence instead of continual declarations of passion. This is presented as Damon’s explicit counsel: 'a Man's general Conduct should be agreeable, without addressing in particular to the Woman he loves.' Anti-pattern: ostentatious professions of passion that invite pity rather than true affection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contrast and timing in courtship (advance when displeasure is present)
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking advantage of moments when a lady is displeased with another or when her imagination is set by contrasts (gayety vs languishment) can be effective; to know when a lady is displeased is often the best time to advance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactical indications: a man who appears cheerful where another is languishing attracts the lady’s imagination; visits timed 'with speed' when the other has angered her; alternating displays of interest/indifference can rebound her affections between the two suitors. Caution: this is described as dangerous and may irretrievably compromise her freedom of choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose company suited to your temper
rubrics_metrics.description: When one can choose companions, one should select those of a temper most suitable to one's own, since the disposition of the head of a family chiefly influences the rest of the household.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how well you and potential companions will bear leisure and solitude (especially in the country where diversions are fewer). Anti-pattern: keeping company that provokes quarrels, peevishness, or constant irritation; such company makes life uneasy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve good-humour in country households with explicit social rules (the 'infirmary' system)
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid the petty squabbles that arise from constrained company in country retirement, proactively institute mechanisms to preserve ease and tranquility, such as an 'infirmary' for temporarily removing peevish members until they show reformed demeanour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rules used by the sender's acquaintance: a wing of the house set aside as an infirmary; any ill-natured words, impatient speech to servants, or signs of dishumour are grounds for temporary banishment; voluntary retirement when one feels an ill-fit is honoured and upon return the person receives marks of esteem if suitably penitent. The society expects petitions and manner of submission as conditions for readmission. This is given as a preventive, restorative scheme rather than punishment alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid and condemn defamation and scandal-mongering
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclination to defamation indicates an ill heart; speaking ill of others is motivated by envy or neglect of one's own laudable qualities and provides gratification to the slovenly and malicious rather than to the virtuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not entertain or spread unsubstantiated reports; Cicero’s admonition is cited: many reports come from those with engagements, ill-will, or natural tendency to slander. When a report lacks a traceable source or credible attestation, treat it as too slight to damage reputation. Anti-patterns: taking pleasure in others' misfortunes, readily accepting and repeating scandal, using anonymous or low-credibility testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require credible sourcing before accepting accusations
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports and rumours should be judged by their provenance: if no one can say whence they had it, or it is attested by someone who forgot who told them, such testimonies are too slight to credit against a person's honour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In defending reputation, trace the report; discount hearsay from low-consideration sources. This is practical guidance for evaluating scandal and protecting innocence—look for concrete attestations rather than chain gossip.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the social mechanics and contemptibility of gossip vehicles
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand how gossips and town intelligencers (e.g., the Lady Bluemantle anecdote) function: they repeat stories without knowing authorship and thus expose the town while offending no single named person directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Awareness: these figures keep news—good or bad—alive by their memory and circulation; they may be always at home and attentive, with stronger memory for old scandals. Response: do not feed such channels; avoid indulging them, and do not derive satisfaction from delaying or broadcasting bad tidings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value fame as the natural follower of merit, not the number of popular votes
rubrics_metrics.description: True fame follows worthy actions as naturally as a shadow follows a body; small minds mistake fame for mere popularity or the quantity of voices on one's side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take comfort that merit, not spiteful or envious tongues, produces lasting reputation. Do not be provoked by virtue; disdain for vice in others is often a symptom of the scandal-bearer's own failings.
